questions.stem: At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreed that:
options: the USA would withdraw all of its troops from Europe at once
Germany would be divided into zones of occupation
the USSR would stay out of the war against Japan
Germany would keep the borders it had held in 1939
questions.explanation: The Big Three agreed to divide Germany into occupation zones, with France given a zone too. Stalin also promised to enter the war against Japan after Germany's defeat, so staying out of that war is the reverse of what was agreed.

questions.stem: At Yalta, Stalin agreed that Poland would hold 'free and unfettered elections'. Why did this promise later add to Cold War tension?
options: Britain annexed western Poland as compensation for its war losses
Poland voted in a referendum to join NATO as a founding member
the 1947 elections were rigged to give the communists control
the USA refused to recognise any Polish government after 1945
questions.explanation: Communist-led authorities used arrests, intimidation and fraud in the January 1947 elections, which the Western powers saw as a broken promise. Poland was never a founding member of NATO; it became a Soviet satellite.

questions.stem: Which change between the Yalta and Potsdam conferences increased tension between the Allies?
options: France had refused to accept an occupation zone in Germany
the USSR had tested an atomic bomb before the USA had one
Truman, more suspicious of Stalin, had replaced Roosevelt
Khrushchev had replaced Stalin as leader of the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: Roosevelt died in April 1945, and Truman took a harder line with Stalin, strengthened by news of the successful atomic test during the conference. The USSR did not test an atomic bomb until 1949, and Stalin led it until 1953.

questions.stem: At the Potsdam Conference it was agreed that reparations from Germany would be taken mainly:
options: by each occupying power from its own zone
as cash paid by a new all-German government
by the USA alone, to help fund the Marshall Plan
through a fixed sum set by the League of Nations
questions.explanation: The Allies wanted to avoid the cash reparations problems after 1919, so each power took reparations in kind from its own zone, with the USSR also receiving some industrial equipment from the western zones. The League had been replaced by the UN in 1945.

questions.stem: The Potsdam Conference placed German lands east of which line under Polish administration?
options: the 38th parallel
the Maginot Line
the Oder–Neisse line
the Curzon Line
questions.explanation: The Oder–Neisse line became Poland's western border, compensating Poland for land in the east taken by the USSR. The Curzon Line roughly marked Poland's new eastern border, which is why the two are easily confused.

questions.stem: During the Cold War, supporters of liberal democracy most strongly criticised Soviet communism for:
options: refusing to become a member of the United Nations in 1945
spending too little of its national budget on its armed forces
denying free elections, a free press and individual rights
allowing far too much private enterprise and profit-making
questions.explanation: Western critics argued that one-party rule and censorship destroyed individual freedom. The USSR was a founding member of the UN with a permanent seat, and it spent heavily on its military.

questions.stem: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948:
options: set a common standard of rights but was not a binding treaty
was a treaty that imposed legal penalties on member states
was vetoed by the USSR in the Security Council
was drafted by the League of Nations before 1939
questions.explanation: The Declaration was a statement of principles passed by the General Assembly, with the Soviet bloc abstaining rather than voting against. Binding human rights treaties, the international covenants, came later.

questions.stem: Which Australian was President of the UN General Assembly when it adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948?
options: H.V. Evatt
Robert Menzies
John Curtin
Ben Chifley
questions.explanation: Evatt, Australia's Minister for External Affairs, presided over the General Assembly session that adopted the Declaration. Chifley was Prime Minister at the time, and Curtin had died in 1945.

questions.stem: In his 1946 speech at Fulton, Missouri, Churchill said an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe from:
options: Berlin in the north to Rome in the south
Warsaw in the east to Paris in the west
Danzig on the Baltic to Athens on the Aegean
Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic
questions.explanation: Churchill described a line dividing a Soviet-controlled east from the free west of Europe. The speech was an early public statement that the wartime alliance had broken down.

questions.stem: The US policy of containment, set out by the diplomat George Kennan, aimed to:
options: overthrow the Soviet government by direct military force
withdraw the USA from involvement in European affairs
share American atomic secrets with the Soviet Union
stop communism spreading beyond where it already existed
questions.explanation: Kennan argued that Soviet expansion could be held back by steady counter-pressure until the system weakened. Containment accepted existing Soviet control rather than trying to roll it back by war.

questions.stem: The Truman Doctrine of March 1947 was first applied by giving aid to:
options: South Korea and Japan
Poland and Czechoslovakia
Greece and Turkey
West Germany and Austria
questions.explanation: Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece, then in a civil war with communists, and to Turkey, which faced Soviet pressure. He said the USA would support free peoples resisting subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures.

questions.stem: How did the Marshall Plan differ from the Truman Doctrine?
options: it was rejected by Britain and France as a form of American imperialism
it funded European recovery rather than stating a pledge
it gave military aid only, while the Truman Doctrine gave only food
it was offered only to countries that were already members of NATO
questions.explanation: The Truman Doctrine was a statement of policy, first applied to Greece and Turkey, while the Marshall Plan funded European recovery so that poverty would not feed communism. NATO did not exist until 1949, and Britain and France were major recipients.

questions.stem: How did the USSR respond to the Marshall Plan?
options: it offered its own large loans to Western European governments
it refused the aid and kept its satellites out of the plan
it accepted aid for Poland and Czechoslovakia but not for itself
it joined the plan but demanded control over aid to Germany
questions.explanation: Stalin saw the plan as American economic domination and forced Poland and Czechoslovakia to turn down invitations. The USSR set up Cominform in 1947 and Comecon in 1949 to bind the Eastern bloc together.

questions.stem: The immediate trigger for the Soviet blockade of West Berlin in June 1948 was:
options: an uprising by East German workers against the government
the introduction of the Deutschmark in the western zones
the building of the Berlin Wall by East German troops
the creation of the Warsaw Pact alliance of satellites
questions.explanation: The new currency showed that the Western powers were building a separate West German economy, and Stalin cut road, rail and canal links to West Berlin. The Western Allies answered with the Berlin Airlift until the blockade was lifted in May 1949.

questions.stem: The Warsaw Pact was formed in 1955 in direct response to:
options: West Germany joining NATO
the armistice that ended the Korean War
the uprising in Hungary against Soviet rule
the building of the Berlin Wall
questions.explanation: When the Federal Republic of Germany joined NATO in May 1955, the USSR formed its own military alliance of Eastern bloc states within days. The Hungarian rising came in 1956 and the Wall in 1961.

questions.stem: The Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship of 1950 increased Western fears because it:
options: ended all Soviet economic and military aid to the new Chinese state
gave the People's Republic of China its seat on the Security Council
allied the two largest communist powers after Mao's victory
gave the USSR direct control over the government of North Korea
questions.explanation: Coming months after Mao's victory in 1949, the treaty seemed to show a united communist bloc stretching across Eurasia. The People's Republic did not take China's UN seat until 1971.

questions.stem: Why did the Soviet atomic test of August 1949 intensify the arms race?
options: it ended the US monopoly on atomic weapons
it was the first hydrogen bomb ever tested
it was conducted over the territory of Japan
it broke the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
questions.explanation: Once both superpowers had the bomb, each raced to build more and more powerful weapons, and the USA went on to develop the hydrogen bomb, first tested in 1952. The Non-Proliferation Treaty dates from 1968.

questions.stem: Mutually assured destruction (MAD) refers to:
options: the idea that a nuclear war would destroy both sides
a treaty between the superpowers limiting the number of their missiles
a US plan to shoot down incoming Soviet missiles from space
the Soviet policy of crushing revolts in its satellite states
questions.explanation: Because each side could strike back even after being attacked, neither could win a nuclear war, which deterred both from starting one. A treaty limiting missiles describes SALT, and the space-based shield was Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative.

questions.stem: The launch of Sputnik in October 1957 alarmed many Americans mainly because:
options: it photographed US missile bases from orbit in detail
it suggested Soviet rockets could carry nuclear weapons to the USA
it carried the first human into orbit around the Earth
it landed on the Moon before any American spacecraft
questions.explanation: A rocket able to put a satellite in orbit could also deliver a warhead across continents, which suggested a Soviet lead in missiles. The first human in orbit was Yuri Gagarin in 1961, and the USA responded by creating NASA in 1958.

questions.stem: Senator Joseph McCarthy's role in the Second Red Scare in the USA was to:
options: argue in the Senate for closer trade relations with the USSR
make unproven claims that communists had infiltrated the government
lead the inquiry that cleared Hollywood of any communist influence
negotiate the armistice that ended the fighting in the Korean War
questions.explanation: From 1950 McCarthy accused officials of being communists, usually without evidence, and many lost their jobs. 'McCarthyism' came to mean reckless accusation; the Senate censured him in 1954.

questions.stem: After the High Court struck down the Communist Party Dissolution Act in 1951, the Menzies government:
options: banned the party by decree using wartime emergency powers
removed the High Court's power to review laws of Parliament
deported all Communist Party members who were born overseas
held a referendum seeking power to ban the party, which failed
questions.explanation: Menzies asked voters in September 1951 to give the Commonwealth power to ban the Communist Party, and the referendum was narrowly defeated. The episode shows how the Red Scare reached Australia.

questions.stem: The Domino Theory held that:
options: a country falling to communism would lead its neighbours to fall
a nuclear war would bring about the destruction of both superpowers
communism would collapse within a few years once its leader died
economic aid to Europe would be enough to stop the spread of fascism
questions.explanation: President Eisenhower described the 'falling domino' principle in 1954, with South-East Asia in mind. The theory was used to justify US and Australian involvement in Vietnam.

questions.stem: The Korean War began in June 1950 when:
options: North Korean forces invaded South Korea across the 38th parallel
Chinese forces crossed the Yalu River into North Korea
US troops landed behind North Korean lines at Inchon
South Korea invaded the North to reunite the peninsula
questions.explanation: Kim Il-sung's forces attacked on 25 June 1950 with Soviet approval. The Inchon landing came in September and Chinese intervention in October and November 1950.

questions.stem: The UN Security Council was able to authorise military action in Korea in 1950 because:
options: China's new communist government cast the deciding vote
the USSR was boycotting the Council over who held China's seat
the USSR voted in favour in order to avoid a much wider war
the General Assembly overruled a Soviet veto by a two-thirds vote
questions.explanation: The Soviet delegate was absent in protest at the Republic of China, not the People's Republic, holding China's seat, so there was no veto. The People's Republic had no seat until 1971 and so could not vote.

questions.stem: According to most historians, the East German government built the Berlin Wall in August 1961 mainly to:
options: protect Berlin from a planned NATO invasion
stop the mass flight of East Germans to the West
separate the British and French sectors of West Berlin
enforce the terms of the 1945 Potsdam Agreement
questions.explanation: Millions had left the GDR through Berlin, draining it of skilled workers. The regime officially called the Wall an 'Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart', but its guns and barriers faced inwards, against its own citizens.

questions.stem: In East Germany, the Stasi was:
options: the Ministry for State Security, which spied on citizens
the national army that guarded the Wall and the borders
the ruling Socialist Unity Party of the German state
the West German intelligence service based in Bonn
questions.explanation: The Stasi used a huge network of informers to watch, intimidate and imprison East Germans. The ruling party was the Socialist Unity Party (SED), which the Stasi served.

questions.stem: Soviet forces crushed the Hungarian uprising in November 1956 after Imre Nagy announced that Hungary would:
options: join NATO and invite American troops in
restore the monarchy under a Habsburg king
hand power back to the Stalinist Mátyás Rákosi
leave the Warsaw Pact and become neutral
questions.explanation: Leaving the Warsaw Pact threatened the whole Soviet security system in Eastern Europe, so Khrushchev sent in tanks. Nagy was later tried and executed, and the West gave the rebels no military help.

questions.stem: Why did Poland in October 1956 avoid the Soviet invasion that Hungary suffered soon after?
options: UN peacekeepers were sent to protect the government in Warsaw
Gomulka promised Poland would stay communist and in the Warsaw Pact
the USA threatened war if Soviet troops entered Polish territory
the Polish army defeated advancing Soviet forces near Warsaw
questions.explanation: Wladyslaw Gomulka won some reforms but reassured Khrushchev that Poland would remain loyal to the bloc, so Moscow accepted him. Hungary went further by announcing it would leave the Warsaw Pact.

questions.stem: After Warsaw Pact forces ended the Prague Spring in 1968, the Brezhnev Doctrine stated that:
options: the USSR would withdraw its forces from Eastern Europe within ten years
only the UN Security Council could approve action within the bloc
the bloc could intervene where socialism in a member was threatened
each satellite state was free to choose its own path to socialism
questions.explanation: The doctrine justified the invasion of Czechoslovakia, where Dubcek had promised 'socialism with a human face'. Letting each state choose its own path describes Gorbachev's later approach, sometimes called the Sinatra Doctrine.

questions.stem: The Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961 was:
options: a failed landing in Cuba by CIA-trained Cuban exiles
a Soviet operation to place nuclear missiles in Cuba
the revolution in which Castro overthrew Batista
a US naval blockade of Soviet ships heading to Cuba
questions.explanation: The invasion was defeated within days, embarrassing Kennedy and pushing Castro closer to the USSR. Castro's revolution had triumphed in 1959, and the naval 'quarantine' came during the missile crisis of 1962.

questions.stem: How was the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 resolved?
options: US forces invaded Cuba and destroyed the missile sites from the air
the UN Security Council ordered both superpowers to disarm completely
the USSR kept its missiles in Cuba and the USA lifted its blockade
the USSR removed its missiles and the USA pledged not to invade Cuba
questions.explanation: Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles in return for a public US promise not to invade Cuba and a secret agreement to remove US missiles from Turkey. The crisis led to the Moscow–Washington hotline and the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty.

questions.stem: The Geneva Accords of 1954 temporarily divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel and planned:
options: a permanent partition into two independent states
French rule over the south until the mid-1970s
a UN trusteeship to govern all of Indochina
national elections in 1956 to reunify the country
questions.explanation: The division was meant to be temporary, but the elections were never held, as South Vietnam's leader Ngo Dinh Diem, backed by the USA, refused. This made the division permanent until 1975.

questions.stem: Australia's involvement in the Vietnam War included:
options: a refusal to commit any army combat units to the fighting
conscripting young men for service through a birthday ballot
a formal declaration of war passed by the Australian Parliament
sending its first combat troops only after the fall of Saigon
questions.explanation: National service men were chosen by a ballot of birth dates, and some were sent to Vietnam, which fuelled the anti-war Moratorium marches of 1970. Australia never formally declared war, and its combat forces were committed from 1965.

questions.stem: Although the Tet Offensive of 1968 was a military setback for communist forces, it was significant because:
options: it ended with the capture of Saigon and the reunification of Vietnam
it led directly to the passing of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
it caused China to withdraw all its support from North Vietnam
it turned much of American public opinion against the war
questions.explanation: Television images of fighting in Saigon contradicted official claims that the war was being won, and President Johnson decided not to seek re-election. Saigon fell in 1975, and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution was passed in 1964.

questions.stem: In the Angolan Civil War that followed independence from Portugal in 1975, the MPLA was backed by:
options: the USA and South Africa
Portugal and its NATO allies
Britain and France
the USSR and Cuban troops
questions.explanation: Tens of thousands of Cuban troops, supplied by the USSR, helped the MPLA hold power. The USA and South Africa supported its rival UNITA, making Angola a Cold War proxy conflict.

questions.stem: Détente in the 1970s refers to:
options: the Soviet policy of crushing reform movements in its satellites
the US plan to build a missile shield in space above America
an easing of superpower tension, seen in agreements such as SALT I
a sharp rise in tension after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
questions.explanation: Détente brought arms limitation, the Helsinki Accords of 1975 and more trade between the blocs. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 ended it.

questions.stem: Which was a direct consequence of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979?
options: the US withdrawal of its forces from South Vietnam
the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics
the signing of the SALT I arms limitation treaty
the signing of the Helsinki Accords on human rights
questions.explanation: More than sixty countries stayed away from Moscow in 1980, and the Soviet bloc boycotted Los Angeles in 1984 in return. SALT I, the US withdrawal from Vietnam and the Helsinki Accords all came earlier in the 1970s.

questions.stem: Ronald Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative ('Star Wars'), announced in 1983, was:
options: a treaty between the superpowers banning weapons in space
a Soviet program to put spy satellites into orbit
a plan to send American astronauts to land on Mars
a proposed system to destroy incoming missiles from space
questions.explanation: SDI threatened to make Soviet missiles useless and to start a costly new arms race the Soviet economy could not afford. It was never built in the form Reagan described.

questions.stem: Which correctly matches Gorbachev's two key reform policies with their meanings?
options: glasnost meant détente; perestroika meant rearmament
glasnost meant collectivisation; perestroika meant purges
glasnost meant openness; perestroika meant restructuring
glasnost meant restructuring; perestroika meant openness
questions.explanation: Glasnost allowed more open discussion and criticism, while perestroika tried to restructure the economy and political system. Together they weakened the party's control rather than saving it.

questions.stem: How did Gorbachev contribute to the fall of the communist regimes of Eastern Europe in 1989?
options: he ordered Soviet troops into Poland to suppress the Solidarity union
he demanded that every satellite state apply to join NATO
he sharply increased Soviet military aid to the East German regime
he made clear the USSR would not use force to keep them in power
questions.explanation: Abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine meant that unpopular governments could no longer rely on Soviet tanks, so they fell one after another. He did not send troops into Poland, where Solidarity won the June 1989 elections.

questions.stem: Solidarity, founded in Gdansk in 1980 and led by Lech Walesa, was:
options: the first independent trade union in a Soviet bloc country
the ruling communist party of the Polish People's Republic
an East German protest group that opened the Berlin Wall
a faction of Hungarian reformers inside the communist party
questions.explanation: Solidarity grew into a mass movement of millions, survived martial law from 1981, and won the partly free elections of June 1989. A Solidarity politician became Prime Minister in August 1989.

questions.stem: On what date was the Berlin Wall opened?
options: 13 August 1961
3 October 1990
25 December 1991
9 November 1989
questions.explanation: East German border guards opened the crossings on the night of 9 November 1989 after a confused announcement about travel rules. The other dates are the building of the Wall, German reunification and Gorbachev's resignation as the USSR ended.

questions.stem: Which event in August 1991 hastened the breakup of the USSR?
options: the explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant
Gorbachev's appointment as General Secretary of the party
a failed coup against Gorbachev by communist hardliners
the completion of the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan
questions.explanation: The coup collapsed within days, discrediting the Communist Party and boosting Boris Yeltsin and the republics seeking independence. The withdrawal from Afghanistan was completed in 1989, Chernobyl was in 1986 and Gorbachev took office in 1985.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the USSR collapsed mainly because of internal economic failure. Which evidence best supports this argument?
options: the large increase in US defence spending under President Reagan
the US-led boycott of the 1980 Olympic Games held in Moscow
the deployment of NATO missiles in Western Europe in 1983
chronic shortages of consumer goods and slowing growth in the 1980s
questions.explanation: Shortages and stagnation come from inside the Soviet system, so they support an internal explanation. Reagan's spending, the boycott and NATO missiles are external pressures, which support a rival interpretation.

questions.stem: The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, signed in 1968, aimed to:
options: limit each superpower's anti-ballistic missile systems
stop nuclear weapons spreading to more countries
eliminate all intermediate-range nuclear missiles
ban all nuclear tests in the atmosphere and in space
questions.explanation: States without nuclear weapons promised not to acquire them, and nuclear powers promised to work towards disarmament. Eliminating intermediate-range missiles was the INF Treaty of 1987, and the atmospheric test ban was the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty.
